key_terms.meaning: A device of two half-cells joined so that a spontaneous redox reaction drives electrons through an external wire.
A tube of concentrated electrolyte (KCl or KNO₃ in agar) that joins the two half-cells and carries ionic current without mixing the solutions.
Pt electrode dipping in 1 M H⁺ with H₂ gas at 1 bar and 298 K; its potential is fixed at exactly 0.00 V and is the zero of the scale.
E° of a half-cell measured against the SHE under standard conditions (1 M ion concentration or 1 bar gas, 298 K).
Metals and couples arranged by E° from most negative (active, easily oxidised) to most positive (noble, easily reduced).
E = E° − (2.303RT/nF)·log Q, giving how electrode potential falls as the oxidised form is used up.
Gibbs free energy change of the cell reaction equals minus n (electrons transferred) × F (96485 C/mol) × E (cell EMF in volts).
Hg/Hg₂Cl₂(s)/KCl reference electrode; saturated KCl version gives +0.242 V vs SHE at 298 K.
A thin pH-sensitive glass bulb whose potential varies linearly with solution pH; used as the indicator electrode for pH.
Finding concentration from the EMF of a cell measured at almost zero current, so the solution is not disturbed.
l/A of a conductance cell, in cm⁻¹; conductivity κ = cell constant ÷ measured resistance R.
A cell whose reaction cannot be reversed; it is used once and thrown away (dry cell, alkaline cell).
A rechargeable cell whose discharge reaction can be driven backwards by an external supply (lead-acid, Li-ion).
Pb anode and PbO₂ cathode in dilute H₂SO₄; about 2 V per cell, the standard car and inverter battery.
Graphite anode and a lithium metal oxide cathode; Li⁺ shuttles between them, about 3.6 V per cell.
A cell that keeps producing electricity as long as fuel and oxidant are fed in (H₂–O₂ fuel cell gives up to 1.23 V).
Storage device using a very high surface area electrode (electric double layer) or fast surface redox (pseudocapacitance).
Metals ranked by measured corrosion potential in seawater, from magnesium (active) to platinum (noble).
A more active metal (Zn or Mg) bolted to the structure; it corrodes in place of the structure.
An external DC supply forces the structure to remain cathodic; a scrap-iron anode is consumed instead.

takeaways: A galvanic cell separates the two halves of a redox reaction so electrons travel an outside wire and do work.
Cell EMF is always E(cathode) − E(anode); a positive EMF means the cell reaction is spontaneous.
The Nernst equation shows that potential is not fixed by nature alone — concentration changes it, by about 0.059 V per tenfold change for a one-electron step at 298 K.
Electrode potentials become useful only against a fixed reference, which is why the SHE, calomel and glass electrodes exist.
A battery is judged by voltage per cell, capacity in Ah, energy density in Wh/kg and the number of charge cycles it survives.
Lead-acid is cheap and heavy; Li-ion is light and costly — the design choice depends on weight and cycle life more than on chemistry.
A fuel cell stores its energy outside the cell, so it never goes flat until the fuel line is closed.
Corrosion is a short-circuited galvanic cell on the metal surface; stop either the anode, the cathode or the electrolyte path and corrosion stops.
Cathodic protection and coatings work by opposite ideas: cathodic protection makes the metal the cathode, coatings simply keep the electrolyte away.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to write the cell reaction, then apply Nernst or ΔG = −nFE, then compare two devices (battery vs battery, fuel cell vs supercapacitor, coating vs cathodic protection) on numbers and on Indian field conditions.

bank.q: Define single electrode potential. Describe the standard hydrogen electrode and explain how it fixes the zero of the electrode potential scale.
outline: Metal dipped in its own ions sets up a charge separation; the potential difference is the single electrode potential
SHE construction: platinised Pt foil, 1 M H⁺, H₂ at 1 bar, 298 K
Half reaction 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ assigned E° = 0.00 V by convention
Any half-cell coupled to SHE gives its E°; sign tells whether it is more or less noble than hydrogen
Limitations: cannot be used in presence of oxidising/reducing species, needs pure H₂

bank.q: State the Nernst equation for a half-cell and for a full cell. Show how it leads to ΔG = −nFE and ΔG° = −nFE°.
outline: Equation with every symbol defined: E, E°, n, F = 96485 C/mol, Q
Cell form: E(cell) = E°(cell) − (0.059/n)·log([products]/[reactants])
Electrical work done = nFE, so ΔG = −nFE
At equilibrium E = 0 and ΔG = 0, giving log K = nE°/0.059
Meaning of positive and negative EMF

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of the calomel electrode and the glass electrode. Give the cell used to measure pH.
outline: Calomel: Hg pool over Hg₂Cl₂ paste in KCl, Pt wire contact
Half reaction Hg₂Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Hg + 2Cl⁻; potential depends on KCl concentration
Saturated KCl calomel = +0.242 V vs SHE at 298 K; it is a reference electrode, not an indicator
Glass electrode: thin glass bulb, internal Ag/AgCl in 0.1 M HCl, potential proportional to pH
Cell: glass electrode | test solution || calomel electrode; EMF → pH
Glass electrode must be soaked in water and handled carefully

bank.q: Distinguish primary and secondary batteries. Define cell voltage, capacity, energy density and cycle life with their units.
outline: Primary: irreversible reaction, single use, dry cell and alkaline MnO₂ examples
Secondary: reversible reaction, rechargeable, lead-acid and Li-ion examples
Voltage in V per cell; nominal vs cut-off
Capacity in Ah = current × time
Energy density in Wh/kg, power density in W/kg
Cycle life as number of charge–discharge cycles before capacity falls to about 80 per cent

bank.q: Explain the electrochemical (wet) mechanism of rusting of iron and state the role of oxygen and of dissolved salts.
outline: Anodic area: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻
Electrons travel through the metal to the cathodic area
Cathodic reaction in neutral aerated water: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂, then oxidised to hydrated Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust)
In acidic water the cathode reaction is 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
Salts raise conductivity and speed up the cell; that is why coastal air rusts iron faster

bank.q: For the cell Zn | Zn²⁺(0.1 M) || Cu²⁺(0.01 M) | Cu at 298 K, write the cell reaction and calculate the EMF. E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
outline: Identify anode (Zn) and cathode (Cu); E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V
Cell reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, n = 2
Comment: dilution of the cathode ion lowers the EMF

bank.q: Write the discharge and charging reactions of a lead-acid cell. Calculate the EMF of a 6-cell battery and explain why the specific gravity of the electrolyte is used as a state-of-charge test.
outline: Anode Pb + H₂SO₄ → PbSO₄ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
Cathode PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
Overall Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
About 2 V per cell; 6 cells in series gives about 12 V
H₂SO₄ is consumed on discharge, so specific gravity falls from about 1.28 to 1.15
Charging reverses every step; never store a discharged battery, PbSO₄ hardens

bank.q: A conductance cell with cell constant 0.50 cm⁻¹ shows a resistance of 250 Ω for a 0.01 M KCl solution. Find the conductivity and the molar conductivity.
outline: κ = cell constant / R = 0.50/250 = 2.0 × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹
Λm = 1000κ / M with M in mol/L
Units check: κ in S cm⁻¹, Λm in S cm² mol⁻¹
Statement that Λm rises on dilution because dissociation increases

bank.q: Describe how the pH of a solution is found potentiometrically using a glass electrode and a saturated calomel electrode.
outline: Cell: glass electrode | test solution || KCl (sat.) | calomel electrode
Glass electrode potential varies with pH; calomel stays fixed
EMF measured with a high-impedance voltmeter at nearly zero current
Calibrate with buffer solutions of known pH (pH 4.0 and 9.2)
Plot or use EMF = constant − 0.059 pH at 298 K
Precautions: soak the bulb, avoid strong alkali, keep temperature constant

bank.q: A steel pipeline buried in wet soil is found to corrode badly near a joint where a copper fitting is attached. Explain the corrosion cell and suggest two control measures with reasons.
outline: Steel (active, E° about −0.44 V) is the anode; copper is the cathode
Small anodic area against a large cathodic area gives very high local current density
Cathode reaction in neutral soil: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
Measure 1: sacrificial anode of Mg or Zn bonded to the pipe
Measure 2: impressed current with a graphite/scrap-iron anode and a DC supply
Also: insulating joint, coal-tar or epoxy coating, moisture control; avoid coating only the anode area

bank.q: Compare lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries for an electric two-wheeler used in an Indian city. Choose one and justify the choice on energy density, cycle life, cost and safety.
outline: Lead-acid: about 30–40 Wh/kg, 300–500 cycles, low cost per Ah, heavy, needs maintenance
Li-ion: about 150–250 Wh/kg, 500–2000 cycles, higher cost, lighter, sealed
Weight and range favour Li-ion for a given range
Cost and recycling infrastructure favour lead-acid for low-cost short-range vehicles
Thermal safety of Li-ion needs a battery management system; lead-acid is more forgiving
Justified recommendation with the conditions named explicitly

bank.q: A campus must store solar power for a few seconds of load fluctuation and also for overnight supply. Evaluate a supercapacitor and an H₂–O₂ fuel cell against a Li-ion battery for the two duties.
outline: Supercapacitor: very high power density, seconds to minutes, low energy density, long cycle life — suits the fluctuation duty
Fuel cell: high energy density, continuous output while hydrogen is supplied, costly and needs hydrogen storage — suits long duration but poor at fast load following
Li-ion: moderate on both, simplest to deploy
Theoretical fuel cell voltage 1.23 V; actual lower because of activation, ohmic and concentration overvoltage
Recommendation: hybrid — supercapacitor for fast response, battery or fuel cell for energy
Mention round-trip efficiency and cost as decision factors

bank.q: Discuss the factors that control the rate of electrochemical corrosion of a metal in contact with an electrolyte.
outline: Nature of metal: position in the galvanic series, purity, grain size, stress
Nature of environment: moisture, pH, dissolved O₂ and salts, temperature
Area ratio: small anode with large cathode corrodes fast; large anode with small cathode is tolerable
Differential aeration: oxygen-poor region becomes anodic (crevice and waterline corrosion)
Passivation: Cr, Al, Ti form oxide films that slow attack; chloride ions break the film
Flow velocity: fast flow removes protective films and raises attack

bank.q: Compare sacrificial anode and impressed-current cathodic protection. State when each is preferred and the limitations of each.
outline: Sacrificial anode: Mg, Zn or Al alloy bonded to the structure; no power supply; suits pipelines, water heaters, ship hulls
Impressed current: DC supply plus inert anode; suits large buried structures and high soil resistivity
Sacrificial anodes need periodic replacement and give limited driving voltage
Impressed current needs power, regular monitoring and risks over-protection and coating damage by hydrogen
Test: structure must be more negative than −0.85 V vs Cu/CuSO₄ reference for steel
Coating plus cathodic protection is better than either alone, because the coating cuts the current demand

bank.q: Explain why a chromium coating protects steel while a tin coating on a scratched steel can does the opposite. Use electrode potentials.
outline: E°(Cr³⁺/Cr) = −0.74 V, more negative than iron (−0.44 V): chromium is the anode and corrodes, protecting exposed steel
E°(Sn²⁺/Sn) = −0.14 V, more positive than iron: tin is the cathode, so exposed steel becomes the anode and corrodes fast
Area ratio sharpens the effect — a small scratch is a small anode with a large cathode
Chromium also forms a passive oxide film
Conclusion: protective metal must be more active than the base metal
Rule: noble coating only works while it is continuous

glossary.def: The study of chemical reactions that produce electricity and of electricity that drives chemical change.
Loss of electrons by a species, which makes it more positive in charge.
Gain of electrons by a species, which makes it less positive in charge.
A pair such as Cu²⁺/Cu that can be interconverted by gain or loss of electrons.
One electrode dipped in its own ion solution, physically one half of a galvanic cell.
The potential difference set up between a metal and its ion solution, measured in volts against a reference.
Electromotive force, the open-circuit potential difference between the two electrodes of a cell, in volts.
For electrode potentials: 298 K, 1 bar for gases, and 1 M activity for dissolved species.
The electrode where oxidation happens; electrons leave the cell from it.
The electrode where reduction happens; electrons enter the cell through it.
Charge on one mole of electrons, 96485 C/mol, written F.
An electrode of known, stable potential against which an unknown potential is measured.
The inverse of resistance, in siemens; for a solution it depends on ion concentration, charge and mobility.
Conductivity divided by molar concentration, Λm = 1000κ/M, in S cm² mol⁻¹.
Shift of an electrode potential away from its equilibrium value when current flows.
The extra voltage needed above the reversible value to drive an electrode reaction at a useful rate.
Two or more electrochemical cells joined in series or parallel to give a usable voltage and capacity.
Electrochemical oxidation of a metal by its environment, which destroys the metal.
Formation of a thin adherent oxide film that slows further corrosion, as in aluminium and stainless steel.
A substance added in small amount that slows corrosion, usually by adsorbing on the metal surface.
Making a metal the cathode of a corrosion cell so that it cannot oxidise.
Depositing a metal coating on a cathode by electrolysis of a salt solution of the coating metal.
